Meiersafe.com collects Mike Meier’s ideas on safety and risk. They draw on his 45 years of experience as a developmental, experimental and production test pilot in hang gliding. Imagine that you need a significant amount of money, with no obvious way to get it, and with serious consequences if you don’t. Someone offers you ten million dollars to play a single game of Russian roulette. One bullet, six chambers, one pull of the trigger. If the gun fires, you’re dead. If not, you get the ten million. How many would take the offer? Mike’s guess, put to the symposium: not many. Yet a go decision that is 99 percent safe, made again and again, carries the same odds sooner than you’d think.

A go decision that succeeds probability of success, percent% of the time, made number of times times, fails at least once 17% of the time: about one chance in 6. The overall chance of success is the chance of each success raised to the power of the number of trials. At 99 percent, eighteen go decisions leave a one-in-six chance that at least one fails, the same odds as the revolver.

Two premises, three factors that work together against good decisions, and a remedy. Two premises. The primary determinant of safety is the quality of decision making. And when a negative outcome could be catastrophic, the go decision must be made only with a very high degree of confidence in a positive outcome. Factor I · Deceptive mathematics. High odds produce long strings of success, and each success seems to confirm the decision. But small risks, repeated, add up: 99 percent, eighteen times, is one chance in six of failure. Factor II · Murphy’s Corollary. If nothing did go wrong, we come to believe nothing could have gone wrong. A positive outcome is taken as proof that the decision was sound, and standards slowly slip. Factor III · The pressure to go. Deadlines, budgets, expectations and ego push us to go when we have doubts. A go decision relieves the pressure; a no-go only increases it the next time. In either case, reinforcement can operate in the wrong direction. The remedy · Analyze your successes. Stay aware of these tendencies, set a quantitative safety metric and a target beforehand, and measure every success against it, to find the ones that were really luck. The framework: why a long record of success can hide real danger Key idea When the consequences of failure are catastrophic, we choose “go” only with very high confidence, so most outcomes are good, and a long string of successes is likely. Each success seems to prove the decision was sound. But success can be partly or wholly luck. Three factors work together to hide that from us, and a two-part remedy helps: stay aware of them, and analyze our successes, not only our failures. On one sheet, to print or email: the one-page handout. By Mike Meier · Edition 1.0, November 12, 2026 (planned) · Adapted from Lessons Learned and Murphy’s Corollary, SETP, 2015 Below: a summary of the paper. Mike’s own words are quoted or labeled.

Sharing lessons learned, with the goal of enhancing the effectiveness and safety of experimental flight test: that’s why the Society of Experimental Test Pilots exists. So Mike’s paper opens with a question: might we be missing something in this process? And a thought experiment. Someone offers you ten million dollars, when you badly need it, to play a single game of Russian roulette: one bullet, six chambers, one pull of the trigger. Would you play? The question in full.

The ideas came out of a serious hang-gliding accident in 1995, on a landing Mike had made successfully some 1,500 times over fifteen years. After a lengthy analysis in which he could find no mistake in how he flew the approach, he was left with one conclusion: the error was the decision to attempt the landing at all. And if that decision was bad, so was every decision to land in the same or harder conditions over the fifteen years before, even though none of those landings had ended badly. The full story: Case study · The 1995 top landing.

The primary determinant of safety is the quality of decision making. When a negative outcome has potentially catastrophic results, the go decision must be made only when a very high degree of confidence in a positive outcome exists.

This section: closely adapted from the paper. When this protocol is followed, it is a natural result that a very high percentage of outcomes will be positive, and therefore also likely that we will see a long string of consecutive positive outcomes. A feedback loop forms: each go decision is validated by the positive outcome as having been a good decision, and is reinforced, and becomes more likely to be made again under similar circumstances. But it goes beyond that. Often the “lesson learned” from a string of successes, even if unconsciously, is that our criteria were unnecessarily conservative: not only were we right to go, but we had margin enough to go under somewhat less favorable conditions. This can lead to a gradual lowering of our standards.
Consecutive successes can mask go decisions that are fundamentally unsound, if the success came partly or entirely from good fortune. Three factors combine to keep us from seeing it.

Below a certain probability of success, repeated go decisions lead eventually to an unacceptable probability of failure. At 99 percent, eighteen go decisions carry a 17 percent chance that at least one fails: one chance in six, the same as the revolver.

Nobody believes Murphy’s Law. But if it were true, so would be its corollary: anything that did not go wrong could not have gone wrong. We are surprisingly susceptible to that belief. We take a positive outcome as evidence that a positive outcome was inevitable.

Deadlines, budgets, expectations and ego push us to go when we have doubts, and to validate the go decision afterwards because the pressure has been relieved. A no-go only increases the pressure next time. In either case, reinforcement can operate in the wrong direction.

entries.h: Why the problem keeps coming back
entries.t: Apollo 1, Challenger and Columbia each followed a long run of successes with a known hazard: pure oxygen at pressure, O-ring erosion, foam strikes on the heat shield. In each, the investigation found a problem that should have been recognized and corrected, and was not. The case studies. None of this is new; the accident reports said it first. What may be worth considering is why these problems seem so intractable. Why did we have Challenger after Apollo 1, and Columbia after Challenger? The Columbia board called for a “new culture” at NASA. I will suggest that as decision makers we can become victims not merely of a culture, but of a deeper and more persistent human psychology. The challenge comes from a powerful combination: the inherently deceptive mathematics of probability, the potentially self-deceptive psychology of judging our own decisions, and the inevitable pressure to go even when we have doubts.

Mike doesn’t claim an answer, but offers two strategies he has found helpful. Be aware of the problem: continually aware of our tendency to succumb to Murphy’s Corollary and to the pressure to go. Analyze successes, not only failures: set a quantitative safety metric and a target beforehand, then measure every outcome against it, to find the successes that were really good fortune. That is what the opening question was pointing at. We share lessons learned from failures, to avoid repeating the mistakes of the past. What we may be missing are the mistakes of the future, the ones we haven’t seen yet. The remedy in full. Deceptive mathematics: why 99 percent, repeated, is not safe enough Key idea Making go decisions at a 99 percent probability of success, we will probably see a long string of successes. And yet after only 18 such decisions, the chance that at least one has failed has risen to 17 percent, or one in six: the same odds as a game of Russian roulette. By Mike Meier · Edition 1.0, November 12, 2026 (planned) · Adapted from Lessons Learned and Murphy’s Corollary, SETP, 2015 Below: a retelling of the paper. Mike’s exact words are set off as quotations.

entries.h: High odds, long strings of success
entries.t: Let’s imagine we’re making go decisions when we have a 99 percent probability of success. Chances are, we’ll see a long string of successful outcomes. Each one feels like confirmation. And yet, after only 18 such decisions, our overall cumulative probability of success has fallen to 83 percent. In other words, our cumulative probability of failure has risen to 17 percent, or one in six: the same level as in the game of Russian roulette. I don’t know how many of you took me up on my offer of ten million dollars with one chance in six of a catastrophic outcome, but my guess is not many.

* This assumes each decision is independent and carries the same risk. In practice, as standards slip with each success (Factor II), the risk on later decisions tends to rise. Raise the probability of an outcome to the power of the number of trials to get the probability of that outcome for every event in the series. At 99 percent, 18 times: 0.9918 = 0.83. The chance that at least one fails is what’s left: 1 − 0.83 = 0.17.*

A go decision that succeeds probability of success, percent% of the time, made number of times times, fails at least once 17% of the time: about one chance in 6. Failure becomes more likely than not after 69 decisions at this level of confidence. 100 crews, each making the same series of decisions On average: 17 of 100 crews had at least one failure. 99 percent, 18 times: the same odds as one round in a six-chamber cylinder. The 99.9 percent for top landings is an illustration, not Mike’s figure. The Rhino Jump is explained in Three Random Thoughts On Safety. Try 99.9, then 99.99. Each extra nine buys about ten times as many decisions before the odds turn against you. It never buys an unlimited number.

entries.h: The data set is too small
entries.t: A long string of successes is exactly what a 99 percent decision produces, so the string tells us very little. Our data set is too small, at least at the beginning of any such process. A landing that fails one time in a thousand averages about a thousand successes before the first crash, and runs of 1,500 or more happen a little more than one time in five. Fifteen hundred top landings without a crash could not show that the landing was safe. Which raises a hard question, one Mike was asked at the SETP symposium: if we can’t reliably tell 99.9 percent from 99.99 percent before the fact, don’t we need 100 percent? Is 100% safety possible?

Murphy’s Corollary: anything that did not go wrong could not have gone wrong Key idea If Murphy’s Law were true, a corollary would also be true: anything that did not go wrong could not have gone wrong. We don’t really believe Murphy’s Law, but we are surprisingly susceptible to an unconscious belief in its corollary. We take a positive outcome as evidence that a positive outcome was inevitable. By Mike Meier · Edition 1.0, November 12, 2026 (planned) · Adapted from Lessons Learned and Murphy’s Corollary, SETP, 2015 Below: from the paper, in Mike’s words, lightly edited; the paper’s indented asides are marked.

entries.h: The law as we quote it
entries.t: The statement of Murphy’s Law that has gone into the popular lexicon is Anything that can go wrong will go wrong. That’s probably not what Murphy said, but that’s how we quote him today. And when we quote Murphy in this way, it is likely that we are doing it mostly for comic or ironic effect. Because to be clear, nobody really believes this statement of Murphy’s Law. Almost anything could go wrong, and if it were really true that anything that could go wrong would go wrong, then most everything would go wrong. And most things don’t.

entries.h: Where it came from: the rocket sled
entries.t: In the paper, an indented aside: material beyond the talk The origin of Murphy’s law is generally attributed to a statement allegedly made by Capt. Edward A. Murphy, a development engineer from Wright Field Aircraft Lab working on Air Force Project MX981 at Edwards Air Force Base in 1949. Commonly known as the rocket sled tests, the project was designed to see how much sudden deceleration a person could withstand in a crash. Paper, notes 1, 2 “Murphy’s laws origin,” excerpted from The Desert Wings, March 3, 1978; Nick T. Spark, “The Road to Murphy’s Law,” Improbable Research, 2003. Murphy had brought a g-force sensor made of a bridge of four strain gauges. The gauges could be wired together in more than one way, and one of those ways would cancel them out and produce a zero reading. After just such a result, Murphy allegedly remarked in frustration, If there is any way to do it wrong, he will, referring to the technician who had wired the gauges. Paper, note 3 “Murphy’s Law,” Wikipedia, accessed September 5, 2015. The basic observation can be found at least 70 years before Murphy’s statement, and likely goes back much further, but today it is almost universally attributed to him.

In the paper, an indented aside: material beyond the talk The statement is obviously false, but only because the common phrasing omits one important word. What the law should say is: anything that can go wrong will go wrong, eventually. Given enough trials, if something can go wrong, it eventually will. The value of Murphy’s observation is not in the relatively pessimistic implication of the Law as it is quoted today, but rather in the more meaningful way in which it informs design – both the design of things, and the design of procedures. What Murphy is really saying is that if we can design out the possibility of doing it wrong, we should. Our lives today are full of examples of this – the polarized electrical plug being just one. The paper’s tragic illustration of the point: Case study · The F-86 aileron bolt.

But if Murphy’s Law were true, if anything that could go wrong really would go wrong, then a corollary would also be true: Anything that did not go wrong could not have gone wrong. Even though we don’t believe Murphy’s Law, we are surprisingly subject to being seduced by this corollary. If nothing did go wrong, then nothing could have gone wrong. We take a positive outcome as evidence that a positive outcome was inevitable. That is what happened with our decision to use top landings to save time in production test flying. We had a long string of successes, and each one reinforced our perception that success was an outcome we could rely on. The problem with that perception is that our data set is too small, at least at the beginning of any such process.

In the paper, an indented aside: material beyond the talk We had many indications during those fifteen years of successful landings that the decision to use this technique was of questionable safety. There were a couple of reasons we chose to land on the upslope of the side of the hill, below the top. One reason was that there was inevitably some turbulence, either rotor or convective or both, as we passed through an altitude of about twenty to fifty feet agl. Being weight shift controlled aircraft with relatively large wingspans and light wing loading (33 foot span, 1.1 to 2.0 lbs per square foot) hang gliders suffer from a progressive loss of control authority and response at lower speeds, especially as one approaches stall speed while slowing down. Approaching from below the top allowed us to approach at high speed for better control, and landing on the upslope greatly reduced the duration of time spent at low speed, reducing the probability of a loss of control. Typically, we would pass through the area of turbulence while still flying fast, then enter a region of wind gradient, where airspeed would drop dramatically as we rounded out to follow the slope of the hill, and then almost immediately flared for landing. Many times, while passing through the region of turbulence and then entering the gradient, I remember thinking, this may not end well. And yet, with each successful landing, my next thought was, well that was fine, no problem – what could go wrong? I had even observed other pilots having significant crash landings, sometimes even damaging gliders, yet I was able to rationalize those as having been due to poor technique – a poorly executed approach path, or poor control of airspeed on approach. It was only when it happened to me, following what I deemed to be a perfectly executed approach, that I was able to realize that my doubts about the safety had in fact been correct, and the suppression of those doubts had been Murphy’s corollary in action. Below: from the 2018 Gulfstream talk, not in the paper. Telling the same story in 2018, Mike added two sentences after the crash landings he had watched: They crashed, but I wouldn’t have. Ego is a powerful enabler of rationalization.

The pressure to go: the hardest factor to overcome Key idea Deadlines, budgets, expectations and our own ego give us a strong incentive to go even when we have doubts. A successful go relieves the pressure, so we are quick to call it a good decision. A no-go only increases the pressure next time. Either way, the reinforcement teaches the wrong lesson. By Mike Meier · Edition 1.0, November 12, 2026 (planned) · Adapted from Lessons Learned and Murphy’s Corollary, SETP, 2015, and the 2018 Gulfstream talk Below: a retelling of the paper. Mike’s exact words are set off as quotations.

If all of the foregoing were not enough, there is one very significant additional factor: the inevitable pressure on us to make the go decision. This pressure can take many forms and have many sources: an impending deadline, a project that is behind schedule or over budget or below expectations, or simply our own personal ego. But it is almost always present in some form. The result is that we have a strong incentive to make the go decision even when we have some level of doubt about it.

entries.h: Reinforced the wrong way, both ways
entries.t: Beyond that, we have a strengthened tendency to validate the go decision as a good one when the outcome is successful, because now the pressure has been relieved. Conversely, if we make the no-go decision, the pressure to go next time typically only increases, as we are now farther behind on whatever schedule, budget or other factor created the pressure in the first place. Below: from the 2018 Gulfstream talk, not in the paper. After a go that succeeds by good fortune We may be positively reinforced for what was, in the end, a bad decision. After a good no-go We are likely to be negatively reinforced, by the increased pressure, for having made the right call. Either kind of inappropriate reinforcement will harm the quality of our future decisions.

In the paper, an indented aside: material beyond the talk I have, over time, come to the conclusion that the pressure to go may be the single most difficult factor to overcome in the pursuit of safety. I have observed in my own decision making that I am far from immune to it, despite the extent of the analysis I have done into its potential for negatively impacting the decision making process in relation to safety. Below: from the 2018 Gulfstream talk, not in the paper. Seven weeks before he was due to present the paper for the first time, at the SETP West Coast Section Symposium in March 2015, Mike launched at sunset in a light wind crossing down the slope, to get the footage that would certify a competition glider in time for the World Championships. The launch failed. He was unhurt; the glider came away with a broken downtube. I was a lot luckier than I deserved to be. The full story: Case study · The 2015 certification launch.

entries.t: In the paper, an indented aside: material beyond the talk Interestingly, it does not really matter whether pressure is real or merely perceived; it has the same effect. In Moonshot, Alan Shepard and Deke Slayton wrote of Skip Chauvin’s decision to decline an engineer’s suggestion to cancel the plugs-out test because of multiple problems: Paper, note 16 Alan Shepard and Deke Slayton, Moonshot (Atlanta: Turner Publishing, 1994), 198. Analyze your successes: finding the mistakes of the future Key idea We analyze failures to avoid the mistakes of the past. What we may be missing are the mistakes of the future, the ones we haven’t seen yet. Set a quantitative safety metric and a target beforehand, measure every outcome against it, and treat a success that missed the target as something less than a success. By Mike Meier · Edition 1.0, November 12, 2026 (planned) · Adapted from Lessons Learned and Murphy’s Corollary, SETP, 2015, Mike’s prepared answers for the Anaheim talk, and the 2018 Gulfstream talk Below: a retelling of the paper. Mike’s exact words are set off as quotations.

entries.h: First: be aware of the problem
entries.t: So if this is a problem, what is the answer? Mike doesn’t suggest he has one, but offers two strategies he has used and found helpful. The first is simply to be aware of the problem: to be continually aware of our inherent tendency to succumb to Murphy’s Corollary, and to the pressure to go forward under less than adequately favorable circumstances.

entries.h: Second: analyze successes, not only failures
entries.t: The second is to expand the source material for our analysis of lessons learned. We tend to share lessons learned from some kind of flight test failure. We analyze these failures and share the lessons in the hope and belief that doing so will help us avoid repeating the mistakes of the past. And that is completely appropriate and worthwhile. At the outset, the paper asked whether this process might be missing something. This is the answer: there may also be ways to identify and avoid the mistakes of the future, mistakes we don’t know anything about because we’ve not yet seen them. That might be done through a careful and critical pre- and post-test analysis of our successes, aimed at finding the successes that were wholly or partly the result of good fortune rather than sound decision making.

entries.h: A metric and a target, set beforehand
entries.t: Before the test, establish a quantitative metric that relates to safety. Set a target for performance, with a significant margin of safety. Measure actual performance against the target. An outcome that didn’t meet it is an apparent success that perhaps should not be considered a success. The target is set before the outcome is known, so the relief of a successful outcome can’t move it.

entries.h: The O-ring seals: how it could have worked
entries.t: This could have been done in the Shuttle program. The 2015 and 2018 talks make it concrete: a quantifiable target for how well the solid rocket booster O-ring seals held back hot gas, with a significant margin of safety. Failing to meet that target would have triggered a stop to the program until the problem was fixed. We can guess why that wasn’t done. The program was underperforming, and the pressure to go, which can exist at many levels within a complex organization, was likely significant. In Mike’s words, Ironically, however, it’s not unlikely that the program lost more time in fixing the problem after the catastrophe than would have been lost to a proactive approach to fixing it ahead of time.

Below: from Mike’s prepared answers for the 2015 Anaheim talk, not in the paper. Asked for an example of a quantitative metric he has used, Mike answered: The two most demanding and dangerous phases of hang glider flight are take off and landing, because of the foot-launched nature of the enterprise, and the consequent small margin between the speed attainable by running, and the minimum speed necessary to fly, and also because of the inherently limited control authority near stall of a lightly loaded weight shift controlled aircraft. I assign a numerical grade to each launch and landing I make, and measure it against a target. When I come up short of the target, I try to figure out where my mistake was, and correct for future take offs or landings. Below: from Mike’s email of October 23, 2026. His scales: Landing quality, 0 to 5 Grade Landing 0 Glider damage 1 Significant glider impact 2 Light glider impact 3 Satisfactory but awkward 4 Good, but less than perfect 5 Just about perfect Launch quality, 0 to 4 Grade Launch 0 Crash on launch 1 Near crash, barely got off 2 Awkward launch, significant airspeed or direction error 3 Satisfactory but less than perfect 4 Just about perfect The target for both is 3. In Mike’s words, anything lower than 3 prompts a re-consideration of all factors and decision making involved in the landing, or in the launch.

If it uncovers decisions or procedures that were flawed in some way, it extends how much our lessons learned can improve safety. The paper’s own closing words: The paper’s conclusion. The 1995 top landing: fifteen years of success, then a crash Key idea Some 1,500 successful top landings proved nothing: the one that failed was flown perfectly, so the error was the decision to land there at all, every time. Read first: this case draws on Warning signs, suppressed, in Factor II · Murphy’s Corollary. In July 1995 Mike Meier was flying production test flights on hang gliders for Wills Wing. To save the long drive back up the mountain, the crew thermalled up after each test and landed on top, near where they had launched. Mike had made that landing about a hundred times a year for fifteen years. Then one day he lost control of the glider in a strong piece of turbulence just before the landing flare, and crashed hard.

Date July 1995 Outcome Hard crash on landing. A sprained ankle and moderate whiplash; with a little less luck, serious injury or death. Proximate cause Loss of control in strong turbulence just before the landing flare. Underlying cause The decision to make the landing at all, repeated some 1,500 times. Factors at work I · Deceptive mathematics II · Murphy’s Corollary III · The pressure to go By Mike Meier · Edition 1.0, November 12, 2026 (planned) · Adapted from Lessons Learned and Murphy’s Corollary, SETP, 2015

Production test flying is the final quality-control check for a manufacturing process that is part science and engineering and part art and craftsmanship. The normal procedure was to launch from the top of the mountain, conduct the test, land in the valley below, then drive back up for the next round, as many as eight times a day. Profit margins in hang gliding are thin. About fifteen years before Mike’s accident, the crew hit on a way to save time: thermal up from launch, fly the test, and land back on top. It saved the drive back up, and it saved one crew member, the driver who would otherwise take the truck down to collect them after each round. Top landing in the early days of production test flying: the gliders already tested wait on the hilltop. Photo: Rob Kells.

Not every launch site lends itself to top landing, but one of theirs did. Still, it demanded precision. Approach into the wind and there are two likely outcomes: too high or too fast and you overshoot, or too low or too slow and you descend into the rotor behind the hill and lose control in the turbulence. The window of “just right” between the two is extremely small. Side view of the approach, not to scale. Redrawn from the paper’s description. Overhead view, not to scale. So the crew developed an alternative: come in half crosswind, more from the side of the hill than from the back, with good speed, and land on the upslope slightly below the top. Approaching fast kept control authority through the turbulence; landing on the upslope cut the time spent slow.

They did this for more than fifteen years whenever conditions allowed, and in that time Mike made probably fifteen hundred or more successful landings. Then one day he lost control of the glider in a strong piece of turbulence just before the landing flare, and crashed hard. For a brief moment after impact I thought I might be dead. For a moment longer, I thought I might be paralyzed. In the end he got away with a sprained ankle and a moderate case of whiplash.

The accident came just before a family trip to East Africa, which gave him three weeks to think about it. He went over every aspect of the approach. The glider was an intermediate model, not very demanding. The conditions were typical summer thermals, not particularly strong. He had done hundreds of landings in stronger conditions on more demanding gliders, and he had flown that approach exactly as he intended. Finding no mistake in the execution left one conclusion: the landing attempt had been inherently, significantly dangerous. The error was the decision to attempt it. And given that most of the top landings I had done over the previous fifteen years had involved gliders and conditions that were as demanding or more demanding, that meant that every one of those other decisions had also been bad decisions. They had been bad decisions in spite of the fact that no bad outcome had followed any of them. The crew did not stop landing on top at once, but they stopped not long afterwards.

I · Deceptive mathematics Fifteen hundred successes felt like proof. But a small risk on each landing, repeated that many times, made a bad outcome likely sooner or later. II · Murphy’s Corollary Each safe landing quieted the thought “this may not end well.” Other pilots’ crashes were put down to poor technique. See Warning signs, suppressed. III · The pressure to go The technique existed to save time and a crew member. Every successful top landing saved time and money, which made the next one easier to choose.

Which routine operation in your program has a long record of success but has never been measured against a safety margin? When did you last think “this may not end well” during an operation, and “what could go wrong?” after it? What quantitative metric and target would tell you that a successful outcome was really luck? What does the routine save you in time, money or crew, and how does that saving shape the go decision? When someone else has a mishap doing what you do, how do you decide whether it was their technique or the operation itself? These questions also appear, with every other case’s, in the Briefing Kit.

The 2015 certification launch: the pressure to go, first hand Key idea A deadline, pilots depending on him and long experience made going feel like the only choice. The launch failed, and the chance he thought might be the last one wasn’t. Together, overconfidence and the pressure to go are a very dangerous combination. Read first: this case is about Factor III · The pressure to go, and how a no-go would only have added to it. This whole case is from the 2018 Gulfstream talk; it is not in the paper. On February 3, 2015, seven weeks before he first presented his paper, at the SETP West Coast Section Symposium, Mike Meier walked a new competition glider down to launch at sunset. The World Championships started in three and a half weeks, and the glider could not compete until it was certified. The wind was wrong and not improving. He went.

Date February 3, 2015 Outcome Failed launch. Mike unhurt; a broken downtube and a scuffed wingtip. Proximate cause Launching in a light wind crossing down the slope, with no upslope cycle. Underlying cause Overconfidence and the pressure of a certification deadline, together. Factors at work III · The pressure to go II · Murphy’s Corollary (overconfidence) By Mike Meier · Edition 1.0, November 12, 2026 (planned) · Adapted from the 2018 Gulfstream talk

The 2015 World Hang Gliding Championships, held every two years, were set to begin in three and a half weeks. The rules required every glider to be certified to the industry consensus airworthiness standards. Wills Wing was under significant pressure to finish certifying its latest competition model so its pilots could compete with the best performance advantage. One step remained: a flight to get onboard video demonstrating longitudinal stability. That documentation requires smooth air, so Mike normally flew it early in the morning or just before sunset, when the air is calm.

When they arrived at launch there was a light upslope breeze. But by the time the glider and cameras were set up, the flow had started to go katabatic, and the wind had turned and was lightly crossing down the slope. He walked the glider down to launch, watching the streamers and hoping for at least a puff of upslope breeze, with the sun setting in front of him. The streamer below alternated between zero wind and 2–3 mph across the slope with a slight downslope component. It wasn’t improving.

I decided it wasn’t going to get any better, and that I might not get another chance to get the footage in time to complete the certification before the competition. I thought about the pilots who were depending on us, on me, to get the glider certified so that it could be flown in the competition. I went for it. Hang gliders are foot-launched, with a minimum flying speed of about 20 mph. They launch by running down a slope, so a launch without a headwind leaves very little margin. More on launching and landing downwind.

The launch, filmed by Mike’s camera on the glider: off the launch, a turn back toward the slope, and into the bushes. 11 seconds. Mike’s verdict: “Bad decision.” He wasn’t able to execute the launch, even though he had thought he would be. Mike wasn’t hurt. Other than a broken downtube and a scuff on the bottom of one wingtip, neither was the glider. I was a lot luckier than I deserved to be. All of my judgments on that day, in that moment, were wrong, in spite of all of my experience in making those judgments.

He did get another chance to get the footage, and got it, and the certification was done in time for the competition. The chance he had thought might be the last and only one wasn’t. In his words, a combination of inappropriate overconfidence and the pressure to go. A very dangerous combination. And it came from the author of a paper on exactly this, seven weeks before he first presented it.

When did you last go because you believed it was your only chance? Was it? Who was depending on you, and would they have wanted you to go in those conditions? What would a no-go have cost you that day, and what did you tell yourself it would cost? What limit, set beforehand, would have made this a no-go without a decision in the moment? Estimate the chance of a failed launch each time you go in conditions like these, with no headwind. Using the calculator, how likely is at least one failure if you make that choice ten times in a career? Fifty? These questions also appear, with every other case’s, in the Briefing Kit.

Apollo 1: a history of success with pure oxygen Key idea A long run of successes with pure oxygen in the capsule made a known fire hazard look safe. There had been previous fires in such environments and documentation of the hazard. The Senate committee concluded that the history of success had led to overconfidence and complacency. By Mike Meier · Edition 1.0, November 12, 2026 (planned) · Adapted from Lessons Learned and Murphy’s Corollary, SETP, 2015 Read first: this case draws on the corollary, in Factor II · Murphy’s Corollary.

Date January 27, 1967 Outcome Fire in the spacecraft during the plugs-out test at Launch Complex 34; the three crew, Virgil Grissom, Edward White and Roger Chaffee, were killed. History of success A pressurized pure oxygen environment in manned space capsules. Warning signs Previous fires in such environments, and documentation of fire hazards in pure oxygen. What was not recognized A complex electrical system in the presence of flammable materials and a significantly pressurized pure oxygen environment was a dangerous condition. Sources quoted Frank Borman’s testimony before the House Subcommittee on NASA Oversight; the report of the Senate Committee on Aeronautical and Space Sciences; Shepard and Slayton’s Moonshot. Factors at work I · Deceptive mathematics II · Murphy’s Corollary III · The pressure to go Below, through “Not recognized as hazardous”: Mike’s text from the paper, pp. 16–17 (with “in the presence of flammable materials” added by Mike, October 2026), with the testimony and report it quotes.

We’d had a history of success with a pressurized pure oxygen environment in manned space capsules, until Apollo One. Had we thought sufficiently critically about it, we might have concluded that a complex electrical system in the presence of flammable materials and a significantly pressurized pure oxygen environment was a dangerous condition. We had even had previous fires in such environments, and we might have drawn on those as evidence of such danger.

But, in the words of Frank Borman, the astronauts’ representative on the Apollo 204 Review Board, in testimony before the House Subcommittee on NASA Oversight, Paper, note 5 Investigation Into Apollo 204 Accident: Hearings Before the Subcommittee on NASA Oversight of the Committee on Science and Astronautics, U.S. House of Representatives, Ninetieth Congress, April 10, 1967, Evening Session, history.nasa.gov, accessed September 5, 2015, http://history.nasa.gov/Apollo204/bormanhouse1.pdf, 81. I don’t believe that any of us recognized that the test conditions for this test were hazardous. Paper, note 6 Ibid., 87. We did not think, and this is a failing on my part and on everyone associated with us; we did not recognize the fact that we had the three essentials, an ignition source, extensive fuel and, of course, we knew we had the oxygen. In the Summary of its report, the Committee on Aeronautical and Space Sciences of the United States Senate had this to say: Paper, note 7 Clinton P. Anderson et al., “Apollo 204 Accident: Report of the Committee on Aeronautical and Space Sciences, United States Senate, Report N. 956,” NASA Historical Reference Collection, NASA History Office, NASA Headquarters, Washington, DC, January 30, 1968, http://history.nasa.gov/as204_senate_956.pdf, 9, 10. It is clear from the Board’s report and the testimony before the committee that this kind of accident was completely unexpected despite the amount of documentation of fire hazards in pure oxygen environments. The committee can only conclude that NASA’s long history of successes in testing and launching space vehicles with pure oxygen environments at 16.7 p.s.i. and lower pressures led to overconfidence and complacency.

The paper quotes Moonshot, by Alan Shepard and Deke Slayton, on Skip Chauvin’s decision not to cancel the plugs-out test despite multiple problems: Paper, note 16 Alan Shepard and Deke Slayton, Moonshot (Atlanta: Turner Publishing, 1994), 198. Time was more important. It was becoming damned critical with all the pressures mounting to get this ship on its way into orbit. More on this factor: Factor III · The pressure to go.

I · Deceptive mathematics A long history of successes felt like evidence that pure oxygen at pressure was safe. A string of successes is exactly what a small risk per test produces, so it says little about the risk itself. II · Murphy’s Corollary Nothing had gone wrong, so nothing could go wrong. Previous fires and the documented hazard were there to read, yet in Borman’s words no one recognized that the test conditions were hazardous. III · The pressure to go In Mike’s words (October 25, 2026): “Pressure to Go was absolutely a factor in the Apollo 1 accident – we were feverishly competing with the Russians and operating under JFK’s mandate to land a man on the moon and return him safely to earth before the end of the decade.” In Moonshot’s account, the plugs-out test went ahead despite multiple problems because “time was more important.”

Which condition in your test program has been present on every success so far, and has never been treated as a hazard? What earlier incidents, in your program or in others, point at a danger you have not yet experienced yourself? Who on your team would say “these test conditions are hazardous,” and when did anyone last say it? Where has a long run of success in your program turned into overconfidence or complacency? Estimate the chance that one of your tests ends in an accident, then use the calculator to see what that chance becomes over all the tests your program has run so far. Does your run of successes still read as evidence of safety? These questions also appear, with every other case’s, in the Briefing Kit.

NASA and Thiokol widened both the blow-by they would accept and the low temperatures they would launch in. The Presidential Commission found they accepted escalating risk apparently because they “got away with it last time.” By Mike Meier · Edition 1.0, November 12, 2026 (planned) · Adapted from Lessons Learned and Murphy’s Corollary, SETP, 2015 Read first: Feynman’s “kind of Russian roulette” is the game in Would you play?, and its arithmetic is in Factor I · Deceptive mathematics.

Date January 28, 1986 Outcome Vehicle lost 73 seconds after launch; all seven crew killed. History of success Shuttles launched successfully with O-ring erosion and hot gas blow-by in the joints of the solid rocket boosters. Response to the successes The amount of blow-by accepted, and the low temperature range for launch, were both expanded. Source quoted The Report of the Presidential Commission on the Space Shuttle Challenger Accident (the Rogers report). Factors at work I · Deceptive mathematics II · Murphy’s Corollary III · The pressure to go Below, through “What could have been done”: Mike’s text from the paper, pp. 17–18 and 21–23, with the Commission’s report it quotes.

We had successfully launched a number of space shuttles with O-ring erosion and hot gas blow by in the joints of the solid rocket boosters adjacent to the external tank. With sufficiently critical analysis, and better internal communication, we might have concluded that this was a dangerous situation before we had one blow up. Instead, influenced by our repeated successes, we actually expanded both the amount of blow by that was acceptable and the low temperature range at which we were willing to launch, increasing the danger of a catastrophic failure.

Quoting from the Report of the Presidential Commission on the Space Shuttle Challenger Accident: Paper, note 8 William P. Rogers et al., Report of the Presidential Commission on the Space Shuttle Challenger Accident, NASA Historical Reference Collection, NASA History Office, NASA Headquarters, Washington, DC, June 6, 1986, http://history.nasa.gov/rogersrep/genindex.htm, ch. V, “Findings” [104]. The Commission concluded that there was a serious flaw in the decision making process leading up to the launch of flight 51-L. A well-structured and managed system emphasizing safety would have flagged the rising doubts about the Solid Rocket Booster joint seal. Paper, note 9 Ibid., ch. VI, “Early Design.” Neither Thiokol nor NASA expected the rubber O-rings sealing the joints to be touched by hot gases of motor ignition, much less to be partially burned. However, as tests and then flights confirmed damage to the sealing rings, the reaction by both NASA and Thiokol was to increase the amount of damage considered “acceptable.” At no time did management either recommend a redesign of the joint or call for the Shuttle’s grounding until the problem was solved. Paper, note 10 Ibid., ch. VI, “Findings,” item 3. NASA and Thiokol accepted escalating risk apparently because they ‘got away with it last time.’ As Commissioner Feynman observed, the decision making was: ‘a kind of Russian roulette. ... (The Shuttle) flies (with O-ring erosion) and nothing happens. Then it is suggested, therefore, that the risk is no longer so high for the next flights. We can lower our standards a little bit because we got away with it last time. ... You got away with it, but it shouldn’t be done over and over again like that.’

In the paper, an indented aside: material beyond the talk The existence and / or perception of pressure was referenced a number of times in the Rogers report. The commission noted for example: Paper, note 14 Rogers et al., Report of the Presidential Commission, ch. IX, sec. VII, “Flight Rate.” The nation’s reliance on the Shuttle as its principal space launch capability created a relentless pressure on NASA to increase the flight rate. Roger Boisjoly, a structures engineer at Thiokol, who strongly opposed the launch of Challenger under the temperature conditions at the time, testified before the commission, Paper, note 15 Ibid., ch. V. I felt personally that management was under a lot of pressure to launch and that they made a very tough decision, but I didn’t agree with it. More on this factor: Factor III · The pressure to go.

One method for doing this [analyzing our successes] is to establish beforehand a quantitative metric that relates to safety, and then to set a target for performance. The target can be set so as to allow for a significant margin of safety. Then by measuring actual performance against our target, we may identify apparently successful outcomes that did not meet our target performance, and therefore should not, perhaps, be considered successes. This could have been done during the Shuttle program in relation to the O-ring seals, and it would have triggered a stop to the program until the problem was fixed. We might guess why that wasn’t done – the program was under performing and the pressure to go, which can exist at many levels within a complex organization, was likely significant. Ironically, however, it’s not unlikely that the program lost more time in fixing the problem after the catastrophe than would have been lost to a proactive approach to fixing it ahead of time. The method in full: A metric and a target, set beforehand.

I · Deceptive mathematics Each flight with erosion that came home safely was counted as evidence. Feynman’s “kind of Russian roulette” is the paper’s own point: a small risk on each flight, repeated, adds up to a large one. II · Murphy’s Corollary “The risk is no longer so high for the next flights.” Flights with erosion came home safely, so the erosion was taken as proof it could not cause a loss, and the standard was lowered: more blow-by accepted, colder launches allowed. III · The pressure to go The Commission found “a relentless pressure on NASA to increase the flight rate,” and Boisjoly testified that he felt management was under a lot of pressure to launch.

Which limit in your program has been widened after a run of successes, and on what evidence? What damage or anomaly do you now call “acceptable” that was once unexpected? If you set a quantitative target for that anomaly today, with a margin of safety, would your recent successes meet it? Where does the pressure to keep flying come from in your organization, and at what levels? When an engineer disagrees with a go decision, how does that disagreement reach the person making it? These questions also appear, with every other case’s, in the Briefing Kit.

Date February 1, 2003 Outcome Orbiter destroyed during re-entry, 16 minutes before scheduled touchdown; all seven crew killed. History of success Shuttles re-entered and landed with damaged or missing heat-shield tiles that had been struck by foam shedding from the external tank. Response to the successes Shuttles continued to launch with the foam shedding from the tank and damaging the tiles. Source quoted The Report of the Columbia Accident Investigation Board. Factors at work I · Deceptive mathematics II · Murphy’s Corollary III · The pressure to go Below, through “Why it happened again”: Mike’s text from the paper, pp. 18–20, with the board’s report it quotes.

We had successfully re-entered and landed a number of shuttles with damaged or missing heat shield tiles that had been struck by foam shedding from the external tank. We might have concluded that the damage to or loss of those tiles created an unacceptable risk on re-entry. Instead, we continued to launch shuttles with the foam shedding from the tank and damaging the tiles, until we lost Columbia.

Quoting from the Report Of The Columbia Accident Investigation Board: Paper, note 11 Harold W. Gehman Jr. et al., Report of Columbia Accident Investigation Board, National Aeronautics and Space Administration, August 26, 2003, http://www.nasa.gov/columbia/home/CAIB_Vol1.html, ch. 6.1. The shedding of External Tank foam – the physical cause of the Columbia accident – had a long history. This raises an obvious question: Why did NASA continue flying the Shuttle with a known problem that violated design requirements? It would seem that the longer the Shuttle Program allowed debris to continue striking the Orbiters, the more opportunity existed to detect the serious threat it posed. But this is not what happened Paper, note 12 Ibid. With each successful landing, it appears that NASA engineers and managers increasingly regarded the foam-shedding as inevitable, and as either unlikely to jeopardize safety or simply an acceptable risk.

From the paper’s discussion of all three NASA cases: In each of these three cases, the post-accident investigation found that a problem had existed that should have been recognized and corrected, and was not. What may be somewhat original, or at least worthy of consideration, are some possible insights into why these problems seem so intractable. Why, after these factors have been repeatedly identified in formal accident investigation reports, do they then show up again in subsequent accidents? Why did we have Challenger after Apollo One, and why did we have Columbia after Challenger? Paper, note 13 Ibid., ch. 11, “Recommendations.” The Report Of The Columbia Accident Investigation Board, among other recommendations, called for a “new culture” at NASA. I will suggest that as decision makers we can become victims not merely of a culture, but of a deeper and more persistent human psychology. I think that as decision makers we face an unexpectedly difficult challenge arising out of a powerful combination of the inherently deceptive mathematics of probability, the potentially self-deceptive psychology involved in evaluating the quality of our own decisions, and the inevitable significant pressure we experience to make a go decision even when we have doubts about the safety of that decision. The three cases: Apollo 1, Challenger and Columbia.

Below: from Mike’s note of October 29, 2026, quoting the board’s report. The board’s report examines NASA’s organizational, historical and cultural factors in its Part Two. Introducing that part, it says: Chapter 6 documents management performance related to Columbia to establish events analyzed in later chapters. The chapter reviews the foam strikes, intense schedule pressure driven by an artificial requirement to deliver Node 2 to the International Space Station by a certain date, and NASA management’s handling of concerns regarding Columbia during the STS-107 mission. More on this factor: Factor III · The pressure to go.

I · Deceptive mathematics The board observed that the longer the foam strikes went on, the more opportunity there was to detect the threat. A long string of safe landings did the opposite: it read as evidence of safety, when it is what a small risk per flight produces anyway. II · Murphy’s Corollary “With each successful landing,” the shedding came to be seen as inevitable and acceptable. The landings that went well were taken as proof that the foam damage could not cause a loss. III · The pressure to go Alongside the foam strikes and management’s handling of concerns during the flight, the board reviewed “intense schedule pressure driven by an artificial requirement to deliver Node 2 to the International Space Station by a certain date.”

Which known problem in your program violates a design requirement, but has never yet caused a failure? With each success, has your view of that problem moved toward “inevitable” or “acceptable”? What would it take for your program to treat a long history of a problem as more warning, not less? Which date in your program is fixed by a requirement rather than by readiness? How would it change your answer to a concern raised the week before? The board called for a new culture at NASA. Which part of the problem would a new culture not change in your own decision making? Estimate the chance that your known problem causes a loss on any one flight. Using the calculator, how likely is at least one loss over the flights you plan for the next five years? Paper, note 4 Chuck Yeager and Leo Janos, Yeager: An Autobiography (New York: Bantam Books, 1985), 185. A tragic illustration of Murphy’s Law was the series of crashes in the F-86s in which a bolt on the aileron cylinder was installed upside down causing the ailerons to lock up under certain loading conditions. The incorrect bolt installations were reportedly traced to one older worker on the assembly line, who ignored the instructions regarding the orientation of the bolt because he felt he knew better how the bolt should be installed.

Murphy’s Law itself The paper uses this case for Murphy’s Law, not for one of the three factors. The bolt could be installed the wrong way, so in enough installations it eventually was. The instructions said which way it went; the design allowed the other way. II · Murphy’s Corollary The corollary is the law turned around: anything that did not go wrong could not have gone wrong. This case shows the law; the 1995 top landing and the three NASA cases show the corollary.

Which part or step in your build, maintenance or test process can be done the wrong way and still look right? Where do you rely on an instruction, rather than the design, to prevent a wrong installation? How would you find out that one experienced person was doing a step their own way, because they felt they knew better? Which of your designs or procedures could be changed so that the wrong way is impossible? Estimate how often a step that can be done wrong is done wrong, say once in a thousand times. Using the calculator, how likely is it to happen at least once across every time that step is done in your fleet in a year? These questions also appear, with every other case’s, in the Briefing Kit.

Hard questions: three the framework raises Key idea Aviation is inherently dangerous, and it often forgives carelessness, but capriciously, so we can’t learn safety just by watching outcomes. Unless we abandon experimental flight test, 100 percent safety is probably not possible. We are not birds. So we had better get as close to 100 percent as we can, with every tool we have. A well-known poster about aviation safety says: Aviation in itself is not inherently dangerous. But to an even greater degree than the sea, it is terribly unforgiving of any carelessness, incapacity or neglect. Mike has always loved the elegant poetry of the statement. It is so beautifully crafted that one could almost miss that it is completely untrue, wrong in just about every way such a statement could be wrong. Take the opening phrase. What is aviation? Suspending oneself at a significant height above the ground, in a 32-foot-per-second-per-second gravitational field, typically at substantial speed, supported only by a waft of air flowing over a wing. An unsupported fall from just twenty-one feet ends at twenty-five miles per hour. A fall from about that height: Mike drops a watermelon from the roof of the Wills Wing building. Video: Linda, 7 seconds. If all of this isn’t the very definition of inherent danger, then I don’t know what would be.

“Terribly unforgiving of any carelessness” implies that any careless act, however small, should reliably bring the most dire consequences. That is not at all what happens. Most pilots know an example of egregious carelessness that led to nothing worse than a good “there I was” story. One from hang gliding: a photo, taken after landing, of a glider that had just been flown with the cable that holds the wings in their spread position held only by a knot in a pull cord, resting in the hole of the metal tang. Had the knot slipped out of the hole in the tang, the wings would have folded together inwards. What you have then is not a hang glider but a lawn dart. The actual consequence was nothing more than some minor embarrassment on social media. The glider as it was flown, Fort Funston, May 2010: the sweep wire held only by the knot in the yellow pull cord. Photographer unknown; published in the Oz Report, used with Davis Straub’s permission. The proper connection, photographed by Mike during test flying; from his 2018 slides. The truth is that aviation is inherently dangerous and that it often does forgive carelessness, incapacity and neglect. But it forgives capriciously, and without any sense of justice. Many egregious acts are rewarded with good story material, while sometimes the most innocent error can cost a life or an aircraft. So we cannot simply practice aviation, casually observe the results, and learn anything meaningful about safety. If we do, we will be deceived. We have to parse the lessons more carefully and more rigorously. That is Murphy’s Corollary, and the reason for analyzing successes. And if the poster were true, aviation would very quickly become very safe, or extinguish itself: those who made mistakes would depart at once, as lessons for the rest. It is the specific challenge of aviation safety that this is not what happens.

There may be a basic, perhaps almost fatal, flaw in the whole idea. A 99 percent probability of success is not sufficient for safety, and it’s easy to conclude that even 99.9 percent is not good enough. But we make safety decisions before the fact. How capable are we of telling a 99.9 percent chance of success, which may not be good enough, from a 99.99 percent chance, which may be? If we can’t do that reliably, don’t we need 100 percent to be safe? And if so, haven’t we just annihilated experimental flight test, and perhaps all of aviation? Mike was asked this pretty much straight out at the SETP symposium. He had expected it, and didn’t have a good answer. In 2018 he said he still didn’t have one, and in 2026 he says he still doesn’t. What he does say is that three things are true: We can improve. The five hundred-odd people in the room at SETP that day suggested they believed it too. We may seriously underestimate the challenge. Without a deep understanding of the deceptive mathematics of probability, the seductiveness of Murphy’s Corollary and the power of the pressure to go, we cannot appreciate how hard it is to improve safety. There is no final victory, only a continuing successful battle. We may not be using every tool we have. That is where a rigorous, critical analysis of successful outcomes comes in. Below: from Mike’s prepared answers for the 2015 Anaheim talk. His prepared answer in 2015 also made clear what he was not arguing: Unless we want to abandon experimental flight test, 100% safety is probably not possible. And beyond that, 100% safety is not a goal that I have intended to promote. Asked at SETP in 2015 whether any risk is low enough, Mike called it the “fatal flaw” in his thesis, and answered: Questions after the Anaheim talk. Below: from Mike’s note of October 25, 2026. Doug “Beaker” Wickert offers a different answer in his 2018 paper on risk awareness. In his view, estimates of the probability of occurrence are essentially worthless; the focus belongs on risk awareness and consequences, and once a possible catastrophic consequence comes to light, the aim should be to eliminate that risk, however small its probability is thought to be. That lines up with Mike’s own question of whether, when the consequence is catastrophic, any probability is low enough to be acceptable. Three Random Thoughts On Safety takes up both ideas.

Below: from the 2018 Gulfstream talk, not in the paper. “If God had meant man to fly, He would have given him wings.” Few aviators agree, and the usual answer, delivered with some smugness, is that we were given the intellect to invent our own. Mike argues the other side. First, the mind of a hang glider pilot. Hang gliders are foot-launched and foot-landed, with a minimum flying speed of about 20 mph, so it’s pretty much necessary to launch and land into the wind. Downwind launches are nearly impossible; downwind landings are highly inadvisable. Two landings, same model of glider, same site, same day. First into the wind; then downwind, shown twice: the glider comes down fast and crashes, and the cows scatter. “Even the cows didn’t like it.” Telluride, 1978. Mike filmed the downwind landing, Tom Tatum the upwind one; the sequence is from Tom’s film, shown with his permission. 42 seconds. Now, a crow. On a windy day, walking in his neighborhood, Mike watched a crow in gliding flight about 30 yards ahead, flying straight downwind at more than 35 mph over the ground, about ten feet up and descending toward the street. At six feet, then three, still straight downwind, his hang glider pilot’s mind was thinking, “He needs to turn now, or this is not going to end well.” And then, at what I would have said was the last possible instant, except that it seemed to be well past the last possible instant, he put one wing up and one wing down, pivoted with perfect precision on the tip of the low wing, and turning into the wind, he put his feet down and landed with zero ground speed, without taking a step, folding his wings as he did so. And then he turned to look at me, as if to say, “What?!” At the 1994 SETP symposium, Dr. Kenneth P. Dial presented “An Inside Look at How Birds Fly.” A fighter as aerobatic as the A-4 Skyhawk has a maximum roll rate of 720 degrees per second. The common barn swallow has a demonstrated roll rate of more than 5,000. The birds, I think, are pretty close to 100%. The birds were meant to fly. We are not close to 100%, and likely never will be. We were not meant to fly. And so if we choose to fly anyway, and want to be safe enough to come back and do it again tomorrow, we had better try to get as close to 100 percent as we can, and use all the tools available to get there. Luck and uncertainty: how luck smears the outcome Key idea Our safety level depends on technical skill and on judgment, and the more unknowns a task has, the more judgment matters. Luck “smears” where we end up, and smears it most when unknowns are many. Reducing unknowns improves safety and also makes our analysis of what happened more accurate. By Mike Meier · First published as “Lucky or Good – Further Thoughts,” Flight Test Safety Fact, Issue 21-09, September 2021 · Full text, with headings added · On meiersafe.com: Edition 1.0, November 12, 2026 (planned) Below: Mike’s 2021 article in full, in his words; the headings are added.

In the May 2021 issue of Flight Test Safety Fact, Art “Turbo” Tomassetti illustrated a favorite theme of his with a colored chart, showing how skill and luck interact to determine performance. Skill and luck together set the level of performance. After Art Tomassetti’s chart in Flight Test Safety Fact, May 2021, used with permission; redrawn for this site. One thing I love about the way Turbo presents his ideas, whether in an article or a symposium paper, is how he goes right to the heart of the matter in such a simple and direct way. Turbo’s ultimate point here, regarding skill and luck, was this: I want both, … but I can only make one. So the best thing any of us can do … is to try to increase our skill. An obvious thought, one might say, and yet somehow, because of the way in which Turbo says it, it really hits home. Another thing I love about Turbo’s presentations is that they make me think. This one made me think a lot, about luck, and about the role luck plays in our performance, our safety and our evaluation of both.

Not being at all shy about stealing from the ideas of others, I began to play around with variations of Turbo’s colored chart, trying to find a way to express how I felt the issue of luck entered into the whole picture. Where I ended up is with the thought that luck is a kind of analogue to “quantum smearing” – the effect by which tiny particles like electrons don’t have a precise location, but more of a smeared probability of where they might be located. Technical skill on the left, judgment on the right, and unknowns increasing from left to right. Mike’s variation on Art Tomassetti’s chart; redrawn for this site. Consider this variation on Turbo’s chart. Here I’ve divided Skill into two components – technical Skill on the left axis, and Judgment (quality of evaluation and decision making) on the right axis. I’ve renamed Performance Level as Safety Level, only because that’s the specific aspect of performance that I’m personally drawn to. And I’ve added a third variable, depicted as a left to right variation: the degree of uncertainty or number/significance of unknowns involved. We can place a point for the level of our technical skill on the left side, and one for the quality of our judgment on the right side, and draw a line between them. Then draw a vertical line – the left/right location of which depicts the level of unknowns or uncertainty we have about the task or project. Then we find our expected safety level at the intersection of those two lines. Few unknowns (left) and many unknowns (right). After Art Tomassetti’s chart. We’ve started with very good technical skill, and good judgment in this example, so our result is also good. What we can also see here is that the degree of uncertainty / number of unknowns determines the degree to which technical skill or judgment will predominate in determining our safety level. If unknowns are few, and our vertical line is situated to the left, then technical skill is the overriding determinant, but as unknowns increase, and the vertical line moves to the right, the quality of our judgment becomes more and more the determining factor. But how does luck fit into the picture?

Luck smears each crossing point: a little where unknowns are few, a lot where they are many. After Art Tomassetti’s chart. This is where the smearing effect comes in. The effect of luck is that we can no longer depend on the intersection of the two lines on the chart to precisely locate our resulting safety level. Luck “smears” the location of this intersection, but it does so differently depending on the level of uncertainty / quantity of unknowns. If the unknowns are few, then not only does technical skill predominate, but the opportunity for luck to play a part is reduced, and the smearing is minimal. If the unknowns are many, then not only does judgment predominate, but the opportunity for luck to alter the outcome is greatly increased. Note that here, in the case where unknowns were high, the smearing effect has both dragged our possible safety level outcome into the caution region, and elevated it to a level above what is commensurate with our level of judgment.

And, of course, these effects feed back into our post event analysis as well. Where luck has a greater opportunity to affect our results, we are more subject to making errors in our analysis of just what was the quality of skill or judgment we brought to bear on the task.

entries.h: Three things we can do up front
entries.t: All of this would suggest that there are three things we can do up front that will improve our safety level. We can increase our skill level, we can increase the quality of our decision making, and we can reduce the number and significance of unknowns. This third one has the additional benefit that by reducing the opportunity for luck to play a part in the outcome, it also improves the accuracy of our post event analysis of what had been the quality of our decision making. Author’s note, 2026. The 2021 text described only the vertical line, though the charts drew both. “And draw a line between them” is added above.
