Three Random Thoughts On Safety: organizational safety culture, the 2D risk matrix and owning the risk Key idea Anyone on a team must be free to say stop. A low probability isn’t a fixed risk: repeated over enough trials it grows, so a green box on the risk matrix can turn red. And to accept a risk, you have to own it: be ready to defend the loss as acceptable when it comes. By Mike Meier · Brief delivered at the joint technical meeting of SETP, the Society of Flight Test Engineers (SFTE) and the American Institute of Aeronautics and Astronautics (AIAA), June 7, 2025 · On meiersafe.com: Edition 1.0, November 12, 2026 (planned) Below: Mike’s 2025 brief, in his words, from his file of October 23, 2026, with his later corrections and spelling fixes. I’m going to talk about three things – organizational safety culture, the 2D Risk Matrix, and something I’ll call “Owning The Risk.”

The subject of safety culture in an organization has been a frequent topic of discussion in the flight test community. The central theme of the 2022 North American Flight Test Safety Workshop was the impact of organizational culture on flight test safety. In the February 2022 issue of Flight Test Safety Fact, Mark Jones made reference to a lack of consensus on the ideal structure of an organization’s safety culture. Art Tomassetti mentioned organizational safety culture in a recent episode of his “On Condition” podcast. On the question of how best to structure an organization’s safety culture, my favorite comments come from remarks Gene Kranz made to his team at a meeting he called on the Monday morning after the Apollo One fire: …we screwed up. It could have been in design, build, or test. Whatever it was, we should have caught it. We were too gung ho about the schedule and we locked out all of the problems we saw each day in our work. Every element of the program was in trouble and so were we. …Not one of us stood up and said, Dammit, stop! What I hear Kranz saying here is that each individual has both the power and responsibility to stand up and say, “Dammit, stop!” So for me, the two most important features of a safety culture are that this be true – that every team member knows that he or she is both empowered, and responsible to flag safety issues, and that the culture be “vertically unconstrained” – such that a team member may escalate safety concerns without limit up the “chain of command” within the safety system. There may be those who will argue that such a structure will lead to a problem of “safety paralysis,” because there will always be some perception of risk that no amount of attempted mitigation can eliminate. The idea of safety paralysis was specifically alluded to during discussions on the eve of the ill-fated Challenger launch when Marshall Space Flight’s Larry Mulloy, in response to Morton Thiokol’s recommendation for a minimum O-ring temperature, exclaimed, My God, Thiokol, when do you want me to launch, next April? I’ll have a suggestion later on for one way to approach this apparent conflict.

The 2D Risk Matrix is an often used way to depict the analysis of the acceptability of risk in consideration of severity of consequence and likelihood of occurrence. In this illustration I have depicted a slightly modified representation of the 2D Risk Matrix. I’ve replaced some of the solid blocks of color with shaded transitions, to highlight inherent uncertainties in assigning probabilities and consequences. Across the top we have varying assessments of probability of occurrence, and down the side variations of severity of consequence. The 2D risk matrix, with shaded transitions where probabilities and consequences are uncertain. There are two things about this that have always bothered me. One is the question as to whether, if the consequence of a negative outcome is catastrophic, is there any probability low enough, except for zero, where the risk can be said to be tolerable? Perhaps my problem here is that the relatively simple visual presentation of the risk matrix suggests a linear decrease in probability along that axis. If the axis were thought of as being logarithmic instead, then maybe I could be comfortable with arriving at a “tolerable” risk within the realm of catastrophic outcomes. My second objection is that it seems to me that there should be a third dimension to risk assessment not captured by the 2D Matrix – the dimension of time – or more specifically, number of trials. A lower probability (that is non-zero) will evolve into a higher probability as the number of trials increases, thus increasing the risk. Thus a risk of significant negative outcome with very low probability may transition from acceptable to unacceptable. In this second illustration I have selected one box – Major Consequence – Improbable Likelihood – and extended it through an increasing number of trials to illustrate it may transition to an unacceptable risk. One box of the matrix, Major Consequence – Improbable Likelihood, over an increasing number of trials.

In the February 2022 issue of Flight Test Safety Fact, Rod Huete, in his Op/Ed: “The Subjective 2D Risk Matrix used in Flight Test,” observes, There appears to be a difference of opinion as to whether the probability of occurrence in the Risk Matrix should be based on subjective judgement (grey bearded approach) or based on a known database (e.g., contain numbers). Rod then goes on to present two opposing views – one from Mark Jones and one from John Hed – in answer to the question. In his 2018 paper, Risk Awareness: A New Framework for Risk Management in Flight Test, Doug Wickert defined a concept of “Risk Awareness” (as an analog to situational awareness) in a way that deliberately leaves out an assessment of the probability of occurrence. Doug writes: To put it bluntly, most probability estimates in traditional risk determinations are worth little more than wild guesses. The probability of a simultaneous loss of engine thrust and asymmetric leading edge slats—the root cause of a 1979 DC-10 crash at Chicago O’Hare, still the deadliest single airline accident on US soil—had been estimated to be less than one in a billion by McDonnel Douglas engineers. And yet those exact failures occurred four times in four years before McDonnel Douglas introduced a fleet-wide fix for the DC-10 in 1982. Recognizing the possible consequences of uncertainty is far more important than providing a dubious assessment of probabilities of potential outcomes. All consequences of uncertainty should be considered regardless of their likelihood. The relevant question for safety boards should be “can it happen” instead of “how likely is it?” The crucial element of risk awareness is not the probability estimate of something going wrong but the awareness that there exist unknown outcomes that must be mitigated. In what might be considered an alternative perspective, in the test program that was the subject of the paper Have You Ever Seen A Rhino Jump, by Michael Wallace and Jonathan Williams, the test team used a Hazard Risk Assessment to compute – based on current fleet experience – a 10−7 probability of a catastrophic engine failure during the fifteen second period between brake release and departure from the ski jump. In this example, the team had what was presumably a relatively robust database from which to compute the risk of a critical failure: the fleet experience.

It is, however, relatively easy to uncover examples of cases where data may have the ability to mislead. As an experiment, I flipped a coin 24 times. I got 12 heads and 12 tails – undoubtedly a lucky result that mimics the overall probability. But that wasn’t the interesting part of the experiment for me. If you watch basketball on television, you will inevitably hear an announcer describe a shooter as being “in the zone” when he makes, say, five consecutive shots, or, having “gone cold” when he misses five in a row. Presumably these are supposedly physical states the shooter enters, in which he either “can’t miss” or “can’t hit” the shot, for some mysterious, but real reason. The best NBA shooters approach 50% shooting percentage, on average, which is conveniently the probability in a coin flip, and they might typically take about 24 shots during a game. The interesting part of my coin flip experiment was that in only 24 total flips, I got one string of five heads in a row (in the zone), and another string of five tails in a row (gone cold). I draw two observations from this. One is that the very concept of a physical state where the shooter is “in the zone” or has “gone cold” is completely unnecessary to explain what we see in a basketball game. But beyond that, one is prompted to consider what we would likely see with a higher probability. If a shooter had a 99% chance of making each shot, we’d expect, on average, to see 99 makes before a miss. But we would likely also see cases of higher numbers of consecutive makes, and possibly 2 or more consecutive misses. This suggests that any data we rely on for predictive value, if we are looking at a subset of all possible data, may be predicting results which are considerably inaccurate or unreliable.

Returning to Doug Wickert’s paper, he makes the distinction between assessments made in the different domains of knowledge, and posits that different approaches are appropriate in the different domains. Where knowledge is high and uncertainty arises out of randomness, calculated, reliable decisions are possible. In the realm of pure uncertainty, where knowledge is low or non-existent, heuristics are more likely to produce the best results. In the case of the Rhino Jump, with respect to the possibility of a catastrophic engine failure during the critical 15 seconds, the probability of success – i.e. avoiding such a failure and the presumed consequent loss of the aircraft – for one trial was 0.9999999 – or “seven nines.” For eight trials, the number in the test program, it dropped only as far as .9999992 – essentially six nines or the loss of one nine. However, if the test program had, for some reason, required 1000 trials, or if perhaps it was proposed that the procedure should become part of fleet operations, where 1000 trials might be expected over the lifetime of the use of the procedure, a success expectancy of seven nines would reduce to only four nines. And perhaps this might not be an acceptable level of risk. At the very least, it might move from the “green” shading into the yellow and might invoke a desire for some further mitigation. The same arithmetic as Factor I · Deceptive mathematics. Try 99.99999 percent, 8 times and 1,000 times, in the calculator. Rod Huete, in his Op/Ed in February 2022 offers this: I personally think the labels of intolerable, tolerable, and acceptable by ICAO are not very practical because in a particular program, you may choose to accept what is tolerable or even intolerable in the ICAO definition.

This leads me to one further thought – the concept of “owning the risk.” For any number of reasons, not all programs will arrive at the same assessment of what constitutes acceptable risk. But what does it truly mean to “accept” a risk? For me, to truly accept a risk it is necessary that one “owns” the risk. Perhaps the greatest failure to do so, in my mind, is represented by the Challenger accident. It is commonly reported (and not to my knowledge disputed), that NASA engineers had assessed that there was a 1% chance of a total loss of vehicle and crew during the shuttle missions. (Specifically, this was a 1% chance per mission, not for the program overall, as a number of references confirm.) Upper management at NASA apparently rejected that probability assessment, and instead adopted one that was orders of magnitude lower (more favorable). The engineers turned out to be right, with impressive precision: out of 135 missions, there were 2 catastrophic failures. One might ask, what could possibly have been NASA management’s justification for overriding the engineers’ assessment of risk? One articulated justification was that the engineers’ assessment did not take into account the fact that safety would improve as a result of everything NASA learned as the program progressed. But did this happen? What did NASA learn that improved safety going forward from the repeated failures of the O-ring seals that led up to the Challenger accident? What did they learn from the repeated loss of heat shield tiles that led up to Columbia? What did they learn from multiple cases of fires in pure oxygen environments that had preceded Apollo One? By the time they had learned anything that changed their policies and procedures, the catastrophic accident that such knowledge might have prevented had already happened. It is one thing to say that the space program recognized and accepted that space flight was risky. The problem with that position is that the response to each of the three major NASA accidents was completely inconsistent with the idea that the risk was accepted. The reaction to each of the three accidents was that they were deemed to be catastrophic and unacceptable tragedies that could not be allowed to happen again. One might conclude that NASA management’s rejection of the engineers’ assessment of risk was, in one sense, a conscious decision not to own the risk. What would it have meant for NASA management to own the risk? What does it mean in any context to own the risk? Well, if one’s most accurate numerical risk assessment says that you have a 1/100 failure probability rate, and you plan to launch more than 100 missions, then you have to expect to have at least one failure. You might not have that failure, but your expectation has to be that you will. Owning that risk means that you should, in a virtual sense, live through all of the logically anticipated consequences of that catastrophic failure: the notification of next of kin of the victims, the funerals, the accident investigation, the testimony before investigative bodies, the justification of the decisions you made as an individual, as a team, as an organization. Owning that risk means agreeing that this will be, when it happens, acceptable. You need to not only be willing to accept the loss, but willing to defend that loss as acceptable, to defend the idea that this is what we all agreed to. And when and if you find yourself unable, or unwilling to do so, then you need to go back and re-examine the chain of decisions that left you with a 1/100 chance of failure. The loss is either acceptable, as a trade-off for what will have been gained by the program, or it is not. If it is not, then the 1/100 number must be changed, or the number of missions severely curtailed. Most discussions of risk focus on how to mitigate it, and most, at the same time, acknowledge that we will never eliminate it. A missing piece that may be capable of joining these two ideas is the concept of truly owning the risk, once you establish just what you believe it to be.

The paper: Lessons Learned and Murphy’s Corollary In brief Presented three times to flight-test audiences in 2015, among five presentations that year: at the SETP West Coast Section Symposium in San Diego in March, the Flight Test Safety Workshop in Scottsdale in May, and the SETP 59th Annual Symposium in Anaheim in September. The San Diego presentation won SETP’s Jack Northrop Award for the Most Outstanding Technical Paper. 26 pages, 16 notes. Written for the spoken talk, with material that didn’t fit the time added in indented italics.

Safety in flight test requires that when the potential consequences of a negative outcome are catastrophic, the go decision must be made only when a very high degree of confidence in a positive outcome exists. When this protocol is followed, it is a natural result that a very high percentage of outcomes will be positive, and it is further likely that we will see a long string of consecutive positive outcomes. When this happens a feedback loop is created in which the go decision is validated by the positive outcome as having been a good decision, and is therefore reinforced and made more likely to be made again in the future under similar circumstances. Beyond that, often the lesson learned from a series of consecutive positive outcomes is that our evaluative criteria for making the go decision were unnecessarily conservative; not only were we correct to make the go decision, but we could have made it under even somewhat less favorable circumstances. This can lead to a gradual lowering of our standards. However, consecutive successful outcomes can mask go decisions that may be fundamentally unsound, if the success is the result, either partly or entirely, of good fortune. Below a certain threshold of probability for success, repeated go decisions will lead eventually to an unacceptable probability of failure. At 99% probability of success, eighteen events results in a cumulative probability of failure for at least one event of 17%, or one chance in six. The common idiomatic statement of Murphy’s Law is: “Anything that can go wrong will go wrong.” This is likely not what Murphy said, nor is it the best statement of the lesson learned from Murphy’s experience, and in fact, no one who thinks about it can actually believe it. Almost anything could go wrong, and if it were really true that anything that could go wrong would go wrong, then most everything would go wrong, and most things don’t. But if Murphy’s Law were true, then a corollary of this “law” would also be true: “Anything that did not go wrong could not have gone wrong.” And while we don’t really believe Murphy’s Law, we are surprisingly susceptible to being seduced by an unconscious belief in Murphy’s corollary – that is, we take a positive outcome as evidence that a positive outcome was inevitable. Combining with our failure to appreciate the nature of probability and our susceptibility to Murphy’s corollary is the inevitable and powerful pressure we often experience to make the go decision under less than favorable circumstances. This pressure is a natural and unavoidable consequence of project deadlines, budgets, and performance expectations. It induces us to make the go decision when we otherwise might not, and to validate the go decision afterwards when the outcome is successful, when that validation may be inappropriate. A means for combating the effects of these three factors is to conduct a rigorous and quantitative pre and post-test analysis not only of failed outcomes, but also of successful ones, with the goal of identifying apparently successful outcomes that may have followed bad decisions, and that were successful because of good fortune.

From the paper, its closing paragraph. A rigorous analysis of successful outcomes would constitute an expansion of our source material for lessons learned. If such a process allows us to uncover some decisions or procedures that may have been in some way flawed, we may expand the degree to which our lessons learned enhance flight test safety. Each case study ends with its own questions. They are collected here so a briefing can draw on several cases at once.

Which routine operation in your program has a long record of success but has never been measured against a safety margin? When did you last think “this may not end well” during an operation, and “what could go wrong?” after it? What quantitative metric and target would tell you that a successful outcome was really luck? What does the routine save you in time, money or crew, and how does that saving shape the go decision? When someone else has a mishap doing what you do, how do you decide whether it was their technique or the operation itself?

When did you last go because you believed it was your only chance? Was it? Who was depending on you, and would they have wanted you to go in those conditions? What would a no-go have cost you that day, and what did you tell yourself it would cost? What limit, set beforehand, would have made this a no-go without a decision in the moment? Estimate the chance of a failed launch each time you go in conditions like these, with no headwind. Using the calculator, how likely is at least one failure if you make that choice ten times in a career? Fifty?

Which condition in your test program has been present on every success so far, and has never been treated as a hazard? What earlier incidents, in your program or in others, point at a danger you have not yet experienced yourself? Who on your team would say “these test conditions are hazardous,” and when did anyone last say it? Where has a long run of success in your program turned into overconfidence or complacency? Estimate the chance that one of your tests ends in an accident, then use the calculator to see what that chance becomes over all the tests your program has run so far. Does your run of successes still read as evidence of safety?

Which limit in your program has been widened after a run of successes, and on what evidence? What damage or anomaly do you now call “acceptable” that was once unexpected? If you set a quantitative target for that anomaly today, with a margin of safety, would your recent successes meet it? Where does the pressure to keep flying come from in your organization, and at what levels? When an engineer disagrees with a go decision, how does that disagreement reach the person making it?

Which known problem in your program violates a design requirement, but has never yet caused a failure? With each success, has your view of that problem moved toward “inevitable” or “acceptable”? What would it take for your program to treat a long history of a problem as more warning, not less? Which date in your program is fixed by a requirement rather than by readiness? How would it change your answer to a concern raised the week before? The board called for a new culture at NASA. Which part of the problem would a new culture not change in your own decision making? Estimate the chance that your known problem causes a loss on any one flight. Using the calculator, how likely is at least one loss over the flights you plan for the next five years?

Which part or step in your build, maintenance or test process can be done the wrong way and still look right? Where do you rely on an instruction, rather than the design, to prevent a wrong installation? How would you find out that one experienced person was doing a step their own way, because they felt they knew better? Which of your designs or procedures could be changed so that the wrong way is impossible? Estimate how often a step that can be done wrong is done wrong, say once in a thousand times. Using the calculator, how likely is it to happen at least once across every time that step is done in your fleet in a year?

Lessons Learned and Murphy’s Corollary on one page Print it with your browser’s Print command, or use the PDF to print or email. Anything that did not go wrong could not have gone wrong. We don’t believe Murphy’s Law, but we are surprisingly susceptible to its corollary: we take a positive outcome as evidence that it was inevitable.

The primary determinant of safety is the quality of decision making. When a negative outcome could be catastrophic, make the go decision only with a very high degree of confidence in a positive outcome. Followed faithfully, this produces long strings of successes. Each success seems to prove the decision sound, and our standards drift lower, even when the success was partly luck.

entries.h: Three factors that hide the danger
entries.t: Deceptive mathematics. At 99 percent, eighteen go decisions carry a 17 percent chance that at least one fails: one chance in six. Murphy’s Corollary. We take a positive outcome as evidence that it was inevitable, and a long run of them quiets the doubts we had along the way. The pressure to go. A go relieves it and a no-go adds to it; in either case, reinforcement can operate in the wrong direction. Chance that at least one go decision fails Decisions At 99% At 99.9% 1 1.0% 0.10% 10 9.6% 1.0% 18 17% (1 in 6) 1.8% 50 39% 4.9% 100 63% 9.5% 500 99% 39%

Stay aware of our tendency to succumb to Murphy’s Corollary and to the pressure to go. Analyze successes, not only failures. Before the operation, set a quantitative safety metric and a target with a margin. Measure every outcome against it. A success that misses the target may be wholly or partly the result of good fortune, and should not, perhaps, be considered a success.

Which routine operation has a long record of success but has never been measured against a safety margin? When did you last think “this may not end well” during an operation, and “what could go wrong?” after it? Which limit has been widened after a run of successes, and on what evidence? What would a no-go cost you, and what do you tell yourself it would cost? What metric and target, set beforehand, would tell you that a success was really luck? About Mike Meier In brief Mike Meier was a developmental, experimental and production test pilot of hang gliders for 45 years, flying the gliders Wills Wing designed and built. He joined the Society of Experimental Test Pilots in 1994 and was made a Fellow in 2026.

Mike Meier. Photo: Brad Hagen. Launching on a production test flight. Photo: Wills Wing staff. Mike graduated from the State University of New York at Stony Brook in 1972 with a degree in physics and a minor in secondary education. After a year teaching physics and physical science in high school, he moved to California in 1973 and took up hang gliding in 1974. He worked at Wills Wing in Orange, California, from April 1976 until the company closed its US operations in 2021, and became one of its owners and one of its three managing partners. In that time he flight-tested 492 prototype configurations, 127 of which went into production, and flew the production test flights of 6,355 gliders. He holds a Master pilot rating from the United States Hang Gliding and Paragliding Association (USHPA) and has been a USHPA certified flight instructor. He is an FAA private pilot with single-engine land and glider ratings. Mike was an Honorary Director of the United States Hang Gliding Association (USHGA, now USHPA) from 1980 to 1997 and served on its Strategic Planning Committee. He was president of the Hang Glider Manufacturers Association from 1982 to 1986, and again from 2003 until the association was dissolved on November 14, 2022. He represented the USHGA on FAA-related committees, among them the Part 103 Users Group at the Riverside FSDO, the ARAC working group in Washington, the USHGA Sport Pilot Task Force, the FAA Part 103 Working Group and the ASTM F37T subcommittee. He was lead technical writer of the ASTM F37.40 task group, which wrote the design standards for weight-shift-control aircraft that the FAA accepts as the airworthiness standards for weight-shift-control light sport aircraft in the United States. From 1976 to 1987 he flew in competitions, was a top-ranked pilot, and flew for the 1981 US team at the FAI World Championships in Beppu, Japan. Origins: where the ideas came from In brief The ideas came out of a serious hang-gliding accident in July 1995, on a landing Mike had made some 1,500 times before. Three years later he wrote them out for Hang Gliding magazine. In 2015 he adapted them for the Society of Experimental Test Pilots, and he has added to them since: on luck in 2021, and on safety culture and risk in 2025. By Mike Meier · Edition 1.0, November 12, 2026 (planned) · From the paper’s Background, Mike’s 2021 letter to the editor and his list of presentations

In July 1995 Mike crashed hard on a top landing during production test flying for Wills Wing. He had been making that landing about a hundred times a year for the previous fifteen years. He could find no mistake in how he flew the approach, which left one conclusion: the error was the decision to attempt the landing at all. Ok. So twenty years ago I had a hang gliding accident that led me to start thinking about how we make decisions that impact our safety. (SETP talk, 2015) The full story: Case study · The 1995 top landing.

Three years after that, I wrote these thoughts out in some detail, in much the same form as I’ve talked about them today, in an article for the national Hang Gliding Magazine. The article, “Why Can’t We Get A Handle On This Safety Thing?”, appeared in the September 1998 issue of Hang Gliding magazine. Read it at willswing.com.

And eventually I began to ask myself whether any of these ideas might have some broader relevance. Mike adapted the ideas for SETP and first presented them at the SETP West Coast Section Symposium in San Diego on March 27, 2015, then at the Flight Test Safety Workshop in Scottsdale in May and the SETP 59th Annual Symposium in Anaheim in September. The paper, Lessons Learned and Murphy’s Corollary, follows the form of the talk. Seven weeks before the first presentation, on February 3, 2015, he made a launch he later judged a bad decision, under the pressure of a certification deadline. Below: transcribed from SETP’s recording, September 24, 2015 (25:17 to 32:01), and lightly edited for reading. Questioners are not named in the recording. Two passages in one question could not be made out and are marked [inaudible]. Question: Not a question so much as an observation. NASA had some of the best scientists and decision makers, and reviews on these programs. Do you think they missed all this, or is it the culture that set them up to do that? Mike Meier: I think that’s a very complex question, and I think they attempted to answer it in the later accident reports. It’s interesting: if you read the Apollo 204 Review Board report, it is almost entirely about the technical issues that led to the fire. I quoted some of Frank Borman’s comments that relate to the decision making, because that’s the point of my paper, but the report itself doesn’t really have any of that in it. It goes on and on about the technical issues. By the time you get to Challenger, they start looking, as Richard Feynman observed, at the decision making. And by the time you get to Columbia, there is a real frustration. I believe it was Sally Ride who was on both the Challenger and the Columbia review boards. There is a whole section in the Columbia accident report where they talk about echoes of Challenger, and they even go back and talk about Apollo 1. Those accidents were on average 18 or 19 years apart, and they all occurred in January or February. We might conclude: just don’t launch anything in January or February, 18 years after the last one. That could be the conclusion. But I think that, yes, they missed it. They missed it because I think two things are true about this process. One is that we’re at a disadvantage because we underestimate the challenge we’re up against. We underestimate the power of Murphy’s Corollary and our susceptibility to it, and we underestimate the power of the pressure to go and our susceptibility to that. And of those two, just observing my own decision making, which is far from what I would even call good, the pressure to go is, for me, the toughest one. Audience member: In my own estimation, I like the corollary: the turtle only makes progress when his neck is stuck out. Question: In the Department of Defense, certainly right now, there’s a lot of desire for innovation in a fiscally constrained environment, and with that, some concern about a paralysis of paranoia. [inaudible] If we could all become experts in stochastic calculus and had a perfect, quantitative view of the risks, [inaudible] As you did the research and reflected on this, what is enough in a risk assessment? Ten to the minus eight, ten to the minus nine? At what point, if we had this quantitative analysis, would we say that’s a low enough risk, and I’m willing to take it for the potential utility of a glider program, or a defense program, moving forward? Mike Meier: I’m going to extrapolate your question a little, because both of these questions have touched on, and I’m going to be up front about this, a fatal flaw in my entire thesis. I’ll tell you what it is, if you haven’t seen it. I’ve shown that 99 percent is not even close to good enough. So we know we have to go at least to 99.9, and then it’s 180 events to get to Russian roulette. Maybe we have to go to four nines, maybe five nines; I don’t know about ten to the minus eight. But the problem is that we’re making this evaluation before the fact. How confident are we that we can tell the difference between 0.9999 and 100 percent? And if we can’t, and the requirement for safety therefore becomes 100 percent, then haven’t we just annihilated the entire field of experimental flight test? That’s where my whole talk breaks down. I have two possible answers to that. I could be flip and just say, don’t extrapolate it that far. But my real answer is that I think three things are true. I’ve already talked about two of them, but I’ll mention them quickly once again, because I know we’re up against lunch. The first, I don’t think anybody here will argue with. It’s very simple: we can improve. The existence of this Society, and the presence of everybody in this room, testifies to our belief that we can improve. The other two come specifically out of my paper, and again I’m repeating myself from the last question. We may underestimate the challenge we face in trying to make that improvement; we may not recognize the full scope of what we’re up against. And we may not be using all the tools that are available to us. Specifically, the one tool I think we may not be using sufficiently, and it’s not that we’re not using it at all, is a critical analysis of successful outcomes, to try to identify those areas where our success maybe wasn’t based on a foundation of sound decision making. That’s the best answer I have. I don’t think it’s entirely satisfactory. It may not be satisfactory at all, but that’s the best I’ve got. Thank you.

The usual chart of risk: severity of consequence, from catastrophic to no effect, against likelihood of occurrence, from frequent to improbable. Mike’s addition is a third dimension it doesn’t capture, the number of trials: a low but non-zero probability grows as the trials increase, so a risk may move from acceptable to unacceptable.

The remedy. A careful and critical pre- and post-test analysis of our successes, not only our failures, aimed at finding the successes that were wholly or partly the result of good fortune rather than sound decision making. It looks for the mistakes of the future, the ones we haven’t seen yet.

Factor I. High odds produce long strings of success, and each success feels like confirmation. But below a certain probability of success, repeated go decisions lead eventually to an unacceptable probability of failure: at 99 percent, eighteen go decisions carry a 17 percent chance that at least one fails, one chance in six.

The decision to proceed. The framework’s first premise is that the primary determinant of safety is the quality of decision making; its second, that when a negative outcome could be catastrophic, the go decision must be made only when a very high degree of confidence in a positive outcome exists.

How to analyze a success. Before the test, establish a quantitative metric that relates to safety, and set a target for performance with a significant margin of safety. Then measure actual performance against the target: an outcome that didn’t meet it is an apparent success that perhaps should not be considered a success.

Factor II. Anything that did not go wrong could not have gone wrong. We don’t really believe Murphy’s Law, but we are surprisingly susceptible to an unconscious belief in its corollary: we take a positive outcome as evidence that a positive outcome was inevitable.

What it takes to truly accept a risk: to live through, in a virtual sense, all the anticipated consequences of the failure, and to agree that it will be acceptable when it happens. Not only willing to accept the loss, but willing to defend it as acceptable. If you can’t, re-examine the decisions that led to the risk.

Factor III. Deadlines, budgets, expectations and our own ego give us a strong incentive to go even when we have doubts. A successful go relieves the pressure, so we are quick to validate it as a good decision; a no-go only increases the pressure next time. Either way, the reinforcement can operate in the wrong direction.

Mike’s picture of luck, by analogy with quantum smearing. Skill and judgment set an expected safety level, but luck smears where we actually end up: a little when unknowns are few, a lot when they are many. The more luck can play a part, the more likely we are to misjudge our own skill and judgment afterwards.

A safety culture in which a team member may escalate safety concerns without limit up the chain of command within the safety system. Mike counts it as one of the two most important features of a safety culture; the other is that every team member knows he or she is both empowered and responsible to flag safety issues.

entries.t: One of the two side tubes of a hang glider’s triangular control frame, running from the wing down to the control bar. The 2015 certification launch
The last move of a landing. The pilot pushes the control bar out to pitch the nose up and stall the wing, killing the forward speed so the pilot can land on their feet. The 1995 top landing
Air flowing downhill under its own weight, usually as slopes cool toward evening. On a launch facing up the hill, it turns a helpful upslope breeze into a tailwind. The 2015 certification launch
Turbulent, tumbling air on the downwind side of a hill or ridge, where the wind spills over the top. The 1995 top landing

Landing on the hilltop you launched from, rather than in a landing area below. It saves the trip back up the hill, but the approach comes in low over the slope, through the wind gradient and any turbulence. The 1995 top landing

How a hang glider is flown. The pilot hangs below the wing and moves their body against the control bar, shifting the center of gravity; the glider pitches and rolls in response. There are no movable control surfaces.
The slowing of the wind close to the ground, caused by friction with the surface. A glider descending through it into the wind loses airspeed as the headwind drops away. The 1995 top landing
Above ground level: height measured from the ground below, rather than from sea level. Murphy’s Corollary
Hot gas leaking past a seal. On the Space Shuttle’s solid rocket boosters, it meant gas from inside the motor getting past the O-rings in the joints between the booster’s segments. Challenger
A rubber ring set in a groove to seal a joint. Each joint between the segments of the Shuttle’s solid rocket boosters was sealed by two of them. Challenger
A ground test in which a spacecraft is disconnected from ground power and runs on its own, as it would in flight. Apollo 1’s crew died in a fire during a plugs-out test on the launch pad. Apollo 1
